KPMG Australia chief acknowledges firm’s ‘indefensible’ actions: Trial Balance

The KPMG offices stand in 15 Canada Square, Canary Wharf on October 2, 2018 in London, England. · CFO.com · Jack Taylor via Getty Images Dan Niepow and Lauren Muskett Mon, August 17, 2026 at 5:50 AM EDT 3 min read

This story was originally published on CFO.com. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO.com newsletter . The Trial Balance is CFO.com's weekly preview of stories, stats and events to help you prepare. Part 1: Amid allegations of client data leaks in Australia, KPMG exec acknowledges "major failings." The Big Four continue to face a reckoning down under. Amid serious discussions to break up the four large accounting firms in Australia, the head of KPMG's business unit in the country told a parliamentary committee late last week that his company has had "major failings" that are "indefensible," according to media reports.

"We can't go with the 'few bad apples' line here, we absolutely have to look at our culture," John Sams, CEO of KPMG Australia, told the committee on Friday, according to Reuters. Sams, who was appointed chief executive after the company's former CEO stepped down amid alleged client data leaks, made the comments at a parliamentary hearing on alleged client data leaks. He said he would not try to defend KPMG's past behavior, Reuters reported. Among the allegations, KPMG Australia's former Chief Operating Officer Eileen Hoggett is said to have printed confidential documents for a client, kept them in her locker and then authorized another employee to view them to help bid on another proposal, according to Reuters. Per The Guardian , the Australian parliamentary committee then read a 2023 email to Hoggett where she suggested showing that employee "the printed version in my locker … without letting too many people know," accompanied by a smiley-face emoji.

Hoggett was expelled from the firm after her email was discovered in July, The Guardian reported. She admitted to printing the documents off and keeping them in her locker, but said she didn't recall letting others see them, the newspaper reported. Deborah O'Neill, who chairs Australia's Parliamentary Joint Committee on Corporations and Financial Services, said that "many, many more" whistleblowers have stepped forward to talk about alleged wrongdoings at KPMG. Meanwhile, a former deputy counsel at KPMG testified that staff "misled" him when he attempted to initiate an investigation into client data leaks. The lawyer said his initial investigation in late 2024 was "fundamentally undermined" by other staffers' "misleading if not directly deceptive" answers, The Guardian reported. The parliamentary hearing came as legislators weigh a host of regulatory changes for Big Four firms in Australia. The nation's assistant treasurer earlier this summer said that some large accounting, auditing and consulting firms had engaged in behavior that was "not fair and honest."
